item.text:
Based on the supplied text, the main drafting and enforcement issues are below. Constitutional challenges are potential litigation risks, not necessarily grounds on which a court would invalidate the bill.

1. **§ 2(1)(A)—“Single training run” permits fragmentation.** A developer could divide training among successive runs, checkpoints, fine-tuning stages, or cooperating models, keeping each below the threshold. The bill does not require aggregation of related training activity.

2. **§ 2(1)(A)—The compute threshold is not a prospective stopping rule.** The text covers a model “trained using” more than the threshold, leaving uncertainty about whether development or training is prohibited before the threshold is crossed. It does not expressly prohibit starting or continuing a run reasonably expected to exceed the limit.

3. **§ 2(1)(A)—Compute accounting is unspecified.** The bill does not specify how to count operations, including sparse computation, low-precision operations, failed runs, synthetic-data generation, or computation outsourced to other systems. Without a consistent measurement standard and recordkeeping, developers can contest whether the threshold was crossed.

4. **§ 2(1)(A)—Exactly the threshold is permitted.** “Greater than” excludes a model trained using exactly 10²⁶ operations. More importantly, there is no margin for measurement error or mechanism for resolving uncertain estimates.

5. **§ 2(1)(A)—The compute threshold cannot adapt.** The threshold is fixed, with no authority to revise it as algorithms and hardware improve. Increasingly capable systems could therefore fall below the compute trigger unless separately designated under § 2(1)(B).

6. **§ 2(1)—Models and systems are treated inconsistently.** Paragraph (A) covers a “model,” while paragraph (B) covers a “system,” without defining either or specifying how coverage follows derivatives. Distilled models, merged models, compressed copies, or products incorporating covered models could have disputed coverage.

7. **§ 2(1)(B)—Capability coverage depends on an affirmative determination.** A system that meets the capability standard is not expressly covered until the Secretary determines that it does. Companies could continue development and deployment while avoiding evaluation or delaying a designation.

8. **§ 2(1)(B)—The capability standard is vague.** “Substantially exceeding,” “human performance,” and “most cognitive tasks” lack benchmarks, comparison populations, or testing conditions. This creates enforcement uncertainty and potentially serious fair-notice challenges, particularly for criminal prosecutions.

9. **§ 2(1)(B)—Dangerous specialized systems may escape.** A system could have extraordinary capabilities in cyber operations, biological research, or AI development without exceeding humans across “most” cognitive tasks. The definition contains no independent trigger for such capabilities.

10. **§ 2(1)(B)—System-level capability is not operationally specified.** The text does not say whether assessments include tools, scaffolding, multiple cooperating models, inference-time computation, or human assistance. Companies could dispute whether the relevant object is a base model or the much more capable deployed configuration.

11. **§ 2(1)(B)—“Secretary” is undefined.** Commerce appears elsewhere, but the bill never assigns the capability-determination power to a specified Secretary. That ambiguity should be eliminated rather than left to inference.

12. **§ 2(1)(B)—Designation procedures are missing.** There are no requirements for notice, evidence, testing access, decision deadlines, publication, effective dates, or administrative review. This invites procedural challenges and leaves unclear when a designation becomes enforceable against a developer or third party.

13. **§ 2(2)—“U.S. person” omits important categories.** It excludes lawful permanent residents and does not clearly include entities organized under federal, District of Columbia, territorial, or Tribal law, or entities other than corporations. Those actors could conduct otherwise prohibited activities abroad without falling within the express extraterritorial prohibition.

14. **§§ 2(2), 3(a)—Foreign subsidiaries and affiliates provide an offshore route.** A foreign-incorporated subsidiary is not itself a U.S. person merely because a U.S. company owns or controls it. The bill does not expressly reach directing, financing, or procuring prohibited foreign activity through such entities.

15. **§ 2(3)—“Advanced AI chips” is undefined.** There are no specifications for capability, architecture, or counting multi-die devices and alternative accelerators. Operators could contest which hardware counts or use hardware outside an asserted interpretation.

16. **§ 2(3)—Chip count is a weak and static coverage measure.** Facilities with exactly 50,000 qualifying chips, fewer more powerful chips, or large amounts of other hardware are excluded. There is no aggregate-compute trigger or authority to update the threshold.

17. **§§ 2(3), 4—Distributed computing can avoid registration.** A company could spread computation across multiple facilities below the chip threshold. The bill neither defines facility boundaries nor aggregates connected sites, common ownership, or coordinated workloads.

18. **§ 3(a)—Key prohibited activities are undefined.** “Train,” “develop,” and “deploy” do not clearly resolve inference, fine-tuning, copying, integration, research assistance, or making model weights available. Different interpretations could leave substantial activity outside the prohibition or undermine fair notice.

19. **§ 3(a)—Supporting transactions are not expressly prohibited.** Financing, selling or leasing compute, transferring weights, and supplying technical assistance are not expressly covered when the supplier does not itself train, develop, or deploy the system. Existing accessory or conspiracy doctrines may help in some cases, but do not substitute for clear coverage, especially in civil enforcement.

20. **§ 3(a)—Foreign remote services create territorial ambiguity.** The bill does not clearly allocate responsibility when a foreign company runs a covered system abroad but serves users in the United States. Whether the provider or domestic customer “deploys” the system in the United States could become a central enforcement dispute.

21. **§ 3(a)—Foreign enforcement mechanisms are absent.** Although the prohibition expressly reaches U.S. persons abroad, the bill provides no specific machinery for foreign records, service, asset recovery, or cross-border investigation. An extraterritorial prohibition is not by itself an effective means of enforcing it.

22. **§ 3(b)—Grandfathering permits completion and indefinite operation.** The exception protects any covered system whose training began before enactment, not merely training already completed. On its face, companies could finish, develop, and deploy those systems indefinitely.

23. **§ 3(b)—A token training start could secure the exemption.** There is no minimum substantive activity needed for training to have “begun,” nor any required contemporaneous documentation. Companies could initiate numerous nominal runs before enactment and later claim broad grandfathering.

24. **§ 3(b)—The exemption has no rule for modifications or descendants.** It does not determine when continued training, fine-tuning, architecture changes, or derivative models become a new system. A company could characterize major future development as continuation of an exempt system.

25. **§ 3(b)—Later capability designations may be neutralized.** The exception appears to apply even if a pre-enactment system is later determined to be superhuman under § 2(1)(B). There is no authority to withdraw grandfathering when such a system becomes demonstrably dangerous.

26. **§ 3(c)—The safety-evaluation exception is unrestricted.** It requires no license, independent evaluator, approved protocol, compute limit, containment, or reporting. A developer could characterize otherwise prohibited training, development, or deployment as safety evaluation.

27. **§ 3(c)—Mixed-purpose activities are unresolved.** “For the purpose of safety evaluation” does not require safety evaluation to be the sole or primary purpose. Ordinary commercial development with an evaluation component could therefore claim the exception.

28. **§ 3(c)—No boundary separates evaluation from improvement or release.** The exception does not prohibit using evaluation to improve capabilities, making resulting weights public, or exposing the system to customers. It also lacks termination conditions once evaluation is complete.

29. **§ 4(a)—Registration scope is geographically unclear.** Unlike § 3, the registry provision does not specify which domestic or foreign facilities it reaches. A worldwide reading would raise jurisdictional and practical problems; a narrower reading could miss overseas facilities operated by U.S. persons.

30. **§ 4(a)—“Operator” and registration timing are unspecified.** Responsibility is unclear for landlords, cloud providers, hardware owners, and tenants sharing a site. There is also no deadline, required registration content, update obligation, or rule for facilities that cross the threshold.

31. **§ 4(b)—Quarterly workload descriptions are underspecified and delayed.** The bill does not require identifying customers, models, compute totals, linked runs, or supporting logs, and sets no report due date. A vague quarterly narrative may reveal little, and a prohibited training run could finish well before a report arrives.

32. **§ 4(b)—Self-certification lacks a verification framework.** No audit, inspection, record-retention, or independent verification duties accompany certification. Facility operators may also lack information about customer workloads, with no corresponding obligation on customers to supply it.

33. **§§ 4, 5—Registry violations lack express penalties.** Section 5 applies only to violations of § 3, not failure to register, late reporting, or deficient reports. General false-statement statutes may address some deliberate lies, but do not supply a comprehensive enforcement regime for § 4.

34. **§§ 2–5—Investigative and rulemaking authority is missing.** The bill does not expressly authorize implementing regulations, compulsory testing, subpoenas, inspections, or access to compute records. Existing agency powers should not be assumed to cover this new prohibition.

35. **§ 5(a)—Civil enforcement procedures and responsibility are unspecified.** The text does not identify who assesses penalties, whether enforcement is administrative or judicial, or the applicable adjudication and review procedures. That omission could produce avoidable disputes over agency authority and due process.

36. **§ 5(a)—The penalty structure may be an inadequate deterrent.** The daily maximum does not scale with compute, revenue, illicit gains, or number of systems, and there is no express disgorgement provision. It also leaves unclear whether simultaneous violations generate separate daily penalties or only one.

37. **§ 5—No express emergency shutdown or injunctive authority.** Monetary and criminal penalties punish violations but do not necessarily stop an ongoing run promptly. The bill should specify available injunctions, emergency orders, and procedures for securing prohibited systems, rather than rely on uncertain background remedies.

38. **§ 5(b)—“Willfully” creates a potentially demanding proof requirement.** Its precise meaning depends on statutory context and judicial interpretation, but it can require proof that the defendant knew the conduct was unlawful. The bill’s ambiguous definitions and exceptions could make that showing particularly difficult.

39. **§§ 2(1)(B), 5(b)—Administrative designation controls criminal exposure without adequate detail.** The Secretary can bring systems within a criminal prohibition under a broadly stated capability standard. The absence of clearer statutory criteria, designation procedures, and notice provisions increases delegation and fair-notice litigation risk.

40. **§§ 5(a), 8—Penalty timing conflicts with the effective date.** Civil penalties purport to reach violations occurring on or after enactment, but § 8 delays the Act’s effectiveness for 180 days. This does not clearly create an enforceable prohibition during the interim and invites disputes over retroactivity and statutory construction.

41. **§§ 3(b), 8—Training started during the 180-day delay has uncertain treatment.** Such systems would not qualify for the pre-enactment exception, but training could begin before the prohibition takes effect. The bill supplies no transition rule for stopping those runs or handling systems completed during the delay.

42. **§ 6—The international obligation is weak and its deadline ambiguous.** “Seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months” does not clearly require negotiations to begin, an agreement to be concluded, or merely an effort to be made by then. There are no interim milestones, progress reports, or consequences for failure.

43. **§ 6—International equivalence is underdefined.** An agreement need only establish prohibitions equivalent to § 3, not equivalent monitoring, penalties, or verification. It could also reproduce the grandfathering and safety-evaluation exceptions without preventing relocation to nonparticipating countries.

44. **§ 7(a)—The early-termination standard and process are unclear.** The provision does not specify the report’s contents, commissioning process, or what “developed safely” means, including whether deployment and misuse risks must be assessed. Nor does it clearly state whether the finding must cover all covered systems or whether evidence concerning a narrower class suffices.

45. **§§ 7(a), 7(b)—The unconditional sunset defeats the safety condition.** The entire Act expires after ten years even without a National Academies report or congressional finding of safety. This also ends the registry and other supporting provisions, allowing companies simply to wait out the prohibition.

46. **§ 7(b)—There is no express savings or wind-down clause.** The text does not address ongoing investigations, pending proceedings, accrued obligations, or records at expiration. Background federal savings law may preserve some liabilities, but an explicit provision would reduce uncertainty.

47. **§§ 2–8—No severability provision protects the remaining scheme.** If a court invalidates a definition, designation mechanism, or application of the prohibition, the text gives no express guidance on preserving independently workable provisions. Severability may still be found, but the omission creates avoidable litigation uncertainty.
